Bedre struktur i lovverket invited to make a formal decision. The bill will also specify the territorial limitations (whether the statute is to apply to Norwegian dependen cies (Spitzbergen, Jan Mayen, etc). Norwegian statutes tend to be rather brief and general. For interpretative purposes, the committee report, government bill and other documents constituting the legislative back ground, are used extensively. The government bill is ref erred to the relevant committee within the Storting, and the discussions within the committee are in practice the more important. The committee may not formally propose new legislation, but may - of course - propose amendments to the bill. The committee will propose the adoption of the bill in its original or amended form to the first chamber with a report discussing the bill ("Odelstingsinnstilling"). The decision of the first chamber is then passed on to the second chamber ("Lagting"), and on its adoption here, the decision is final. Special constitutional procedures cover situations in which the two chambers disagree. Part of the preparatory work within the ad ministration is a review by the Legislative De partment of the Ministry of Justice. This review addresses the formal elements of the bill, and checks how it relates to other statutes in force. The Department can only give advice, but its re putation ensures that its points are tåken into account by the agency promoting the bill. As a point of interest one might note that there is today no formal training in how to draft legislation, neither at the universities, nor within the administration itself. There is, however, a two-day seminar offered by one of the professional societies. The structure of a Norwegian statute is hi erarchical. The statute is divided into "secti ons" (traditionally indicated by the "§"- cha racter). 5) The sections may be grouped in chapters or parts, and are generally assigned sequential numbers, though some are assigned numbers indicating the chapter and the secti on within the chapter. The parliament has no organized access to legislative resources. The committees have se cretaries, but there are no special secretariats or other arrangements which assist with re spect to legislative reform. The decision of the Storting is then passed on to the King for sanction and lodged with the Office of the Prime Minister, which keeps track of the adopted statutes passed on from the Storting. The Royal Assent has no real po litical function today, but is retained as a matter of form. The day of sanction marks also the date of the statute, each statute is as signed a unique identifier composed of a se quential number within the calendar year. A section is sub-divided into paragraphs. There may be further sub-divisions into num bers or letters, and the use of these are not al ways consistent. Fig 3 - Basic structure of a statute Statutes may contain a provision specify ing when its provisions enter into force. Or there may be a clause delegating to the King in Council to decide this. Normally there will be a short interval to take the necessary admi nistrative action preparatory to the imple mentation of the law, but in exceptional cases there may be a prolonged delay. The current statute which has been waiting longest for its entry into force is a statute of June 17, 1966 no 2 on hovercrafts. More than 25 years have passed since its adoption without the statute entering into force. There is no systematic ta ble or procedure for identifying which statu tes - or parts of statutes - are still pending en try into force. The Storting may also take plenary decisi ons provided they do not contravene the prin ciple of legality and are within the bounds of the Constitution and the statutes. They are ranked below statutes, but above other decisi ons. Today these plenary decisions are not pu blished in a special series or compilation, but only as part of the proceedings of the Storting. 5) This is in Norwegian called a "paragraf", which explains why there is a tendency for Norwegians to confuse a paragraph of a section with the secti on itself. The King has according to the Constitution the power to adopt provisional ordinances,

Vedlegg 29 There is a further type of legal provision termed "instructions". These are provisions drawn up by a superior authority within the public administration which outline the orga nization or procedures to be adopted by its subordinated agencies. mainly to take action when the Storting is not in session. They had an important function at the time the Storting did not meet every year, but today on average only one provisional or dinance is passed annually. During the Se cond World War, however, when the parlia ment for obvious reasons did not meet, the provisional ordinances again became very useful. They are ranked as statutes, but have only temporary effect. Guidelines and other explanatory material are also published. They may be decisive for the practice of law in the administration, but they do not have any formal status. Regulations are defined in the Public Admi nistration Act as general rules as opposed to de cisions in a case. The definition is based on the substantive content of the decision, and the na ture of a decision is consequently not always obvious. To a large extent they rely on statutory authority, but this is no prerequisite when not in conflict with the "principle of legality". To the extent that Norway has obligations under international law, it is assumed that Norwegian internal law is in compliance with such obligations. The national provision, for instance in a treaty, is, however, not directly applicable in a Norwegian court of law until it has been formally incorporated through an act of parliament. As a result of the European Economic Area agreement, Norway will have to adjust its laws to those of the European Community. It is estimated that 100 statutes will have to be amended to comply with the Community re quirements. However, for some time it has been a requirement to take into account Com munity Law before drafting new statutes and where there are deviations to identify and ex plain them. The initiative for new regulations may be tåken by different actors within the legal or political system. There is no general procedure governing the preparation and drafting of re gulations. The proposed regulations are only rarely prepared by a committee publishing a report. Simple regulations are typically draf ted by one person or a small group. More com plex regulations are typically prepared by in ter-ministerial working parties. The proposed regulations should be reviewed with respect to cost impact on the public and the private sec tor, and the administrative consequences of implementing the regulation. Unlike the pro cedures governing the preparation of statutes, the text of a regulation does not have to be examined by legal draftsmen. PUBLICATION OF STATUTES AND REGULATIONS Statutes are not published as such by the Storting, though they will be included in the published proceedings. In addition, the office of the Storting publishes at the end of each session a compilation of the statutes adopted and sanctioned during that session. In this case, the statutes are published exactly as adopted. For instance, a statute amending a prior statute will be published as a text requi ring that the amendment should take place rather as a Consolidated text, where the amendments have been integrated in the amended statute. There are no legal conse quences related to the publication of the ses sional compilation. The regulation has to include an explicit reference to the statute from which it derives its authority, and nåme the administrative agency responsible for issuing the regulation. This is an important requirement for regulato ry management, and the resources necessary to secure explicit and correct citation chains are considerable. A proposed regulation has to be made avai lable for comment or "hearing" to interested parties - the relevant ministries, public and private institutions and organisations. The consultative period of "hearing" is generally three months, and should not be less than six weeks. The offlcial publication of statutes is left to the government, related to the formal sanction of the King. Also regulations and other provi sions are published by the government. Regulations are traditionally drafted along similar lines to statutes. The normal publication is the Official Le gal Gazette (Norsk Lovtidend), which is governed by a statute specifying what has to be published and the consequences of the publication (Statute of June 19, 1969 no 53). The Legal Gazette is published in two series, Series I contains legislative provisions appli cable to the whole country, Series II contains local or regional provisions. The gazette is Regulations are also issued by local or regi onal authorities. Regulations have to be published in the le gal gazette or in other appropriate publicati ons, otherwise they are not valid with respect to the members of the public. The Office of the Prime Minister has issued instructions for the publication of regulations, and their drafting.

publicati ons, otherwise they are not valid with respect to the members of the public. The Office of the Prime Minister has issued instructions for the publication of regulations, and their drafting.

For provisional regulations, or regulations concer ning a specific event, publication may be wholly omitted - if not considered appropriate - publication should then take the form of no tification in newspapers, advertisements, bro adcasting, etc. There is also authority under the statute to exempt regulations within cer tain areas from the duty to publish in the Le gal Gazette. This has then to be authorized by the King in Council. Traditionally the editorial responsibility has been that of the Office of the Prime Minister, but recently (May 1, 1992) the responsibility has been transf erred to the Ministry of Justice. Statutes are published as they are enacted, as in the sessional compilation of the Storting, with only some minor, mainly bibliographical additions. There are no formal rules on when publication should take place, but this offers few problems: The Office of the Prime Minis ter keeps track of which statutes have been approved, and måkes them available for pu blication. Generally the statutes are published one or two weeks after the Royal Assent, though delays may increase in the busy final period of the spring- and autumn sessions. Regulations which are not published, may also escape inclusion in the data base. A more severe problem than those regulations for which an explicit exception is made, is those which by omission or error fail to be publis hed. It is estimated that of 4 179 regulations 695 (ie 17 per cent) were not published after 1970 and 122 (ie 3 per cent) after 1980. It is considered that this is an undesirable situa tion which ought to be remedied. Publication of the statute is not a prerequi site for the statute taking effect with respect to the general public. Consequently, if the sta tute has an entry-into-force clause specifying that the statute should take effect "at once", the statute will enter into force on the date of the sanction, but there will still be a delay of weeks bef ore it is actually published. Other provisions. In principle other provi sions or decisions may be published in the Le gal Gazette, but the only type published in ad dition to statutes and regulation are decisions to delegate authority to issue regulations un der a statute. If a statute lacks an explicit clause gover ning its entry into force (which it rarely will), it enters into force one month after its publi cation in the Official Legal Gazette.

un der a statute. If a statute lacks an explicit clause gover ning its entry into force (which it rarely will), it enters into force one month after its publi cation in the Official Legal Gazette.
In this case, there is no record in the Legal Gazette of the date on which the provision entered into force, and this may be somewhat difficult to determine. The compilation of statutes in for ce will, however, include a footnote specifying the date also in these cases. Other publication methods. There are seve ral major publication schemes in addition to the Legal Gazette through news-letters pu blished by an agency. There are, however, no rules on the publication outside or in addition to the Official Legal Gazette. In practice the most important publication is the bi-annual, one-volume publication of statutes in force ("Norges Lover"). This is semi-official, and contains in principle all sta tutes in Consolidated form. The statutes are organised chronologically, there is a subject and an alphabetical index as well as editorial cross-references. For each statute, the regula tions issued under its authority are specified, and a reference to the title specifies the legis lative history. Decisions to make a statute effective have to be published in the Legal Gazette. This does not cause any problems when the decisi on is made by the King in Council. If, how ever, authority to decide on the entry into for ce is delegated to a subordinate agency, the editor of the gazette has to rely on that agency to communicate its decision for publication. This occasionally fails to happen. A recent example is the Statute of March 15, 1991 no 2 on the Government Security Fund for Banks which was meant to enter into force on March 25, 1991. This decision was not published un til November 22, 1991. This is supplemented by the multi-volume compilation of regulations in force, also in Consolidated form. The publications have two different, private publishers. Both are based on the data bases maintained by the Lawdata foundation, which also assists the government on a contract basis with the publication of the Official Legal Ga zette. In this way, information technology has provided a means for an integration of the tra ditional legal information schemes. Regulations have to be published according to the Public Administration Act (section 38, first paragraph, letter a). The procedure is rat her similar to that for statutes, but the duty to publish the regulations has some modificati ons. It may be sufficient to publish a note summarizing the regulation and indicating from which source the full text is available; this possibility is not frequently used, and then only for voluminous regulations of a Effect of non-publication.

the regulation and indicating from which source the full text is available; this possibility is not frequently used, and then only for voluminous regulations of a Effect of non-publication.
As mentioned above, the publication of a statute determines the date on which the statute enters into force when the statute itself does not specify such a

side 445

Bedre struktur i lovverket date. Apart from this, the failure to publish a statute does not have any legal effect - it is not a condition for the statute' s entry into force. MAIN OBJECTIVES OF THE COMMITTEE The main challenge for Norwegian legislation is its accessibility or availability. There are diffi culties in retrieving some of the provisions, and the associated costs are high. In addition, much of the legislation is difficult to research and un derstand. In total this creates a high threshold for gaining insight into the law. For the regulations, the Public Administra tion Act (section 39) emphazises this principle. The decisive factor is whether the person in question had knowledge of the provisions. If the person has such knowledge, he or she may not use as a defence the argument that the provisions were not published. But if a regula tion is not published in the Legal Gazette, and has not otherwise come to the knowledge of the person in question, the regulation cannot be applied with a detrimental effect. The ideal objective should be that statutes and regulations are drafted in such a way that their contents are understood by those subject to the rules - the citizens, business people, counsellors and the public administration - as precisely as possible, with the lowest possible expenditure in terms of time, money or effort. Textual clarity, high consistency in the provisi ons and a structure easy to understand and to which the user may relate, are the most impor tant requirements. For the individual, the cru cial test is the expenditure necessary to identif y the legal instrument relevant to him or her in an actual problem situation, or with respect to an actual activity , and how easy it is to find and un derstand the relevant provisions. Regulatory management. Availability of re gulations was considerably improved with the establishment of a regulatory data base in the 1980 s. The statutes were already available in the bi-annual compilation of statutes in force, which also became the basis of the first legal data base. In practice availability is today quite good, but there are limitations, since not all regulations are published in the Legal Ga zette, and consequently escape integration in the data bases. Also, there may be older un identified regulations. The first report of the committee mainly addressed what statutes could be repealed as håving lost their function. This, the second re port, is mainly concerned with the structure of the legislation. The data bases are maintained by the Law data foundation, an independent, non-profit organisation governed by a board represen ting the government (the Ministry of Justice and the Ministry of Labour and Government Administration), the professional bodies (the Bar Association and the Association of Jud ges), and the universities (the Faculty of Law, Oslo). In addition to the data bases, Lawdata has released a trial CD-ROM, and will from 1992 offer a CD-ROM subscription scheme. The key to the work of the committee has been to tidy up the legislation, and create a more appropriate structure. The legislation has been viewed as a whole. The quality and value of the legislation as an information system has been the f ocal point, combined with a desire to secure a satisf actory standard of the provisions. In spite of this, statutes and regulations are far from easily available - the provisions may be difficult to locate and understand. The ef fects of this are several: Increased costs for le gal research in the public and the private sec tor and reduced compliance. The fragmented nature of the provisions also måkes it more difficult to relate to them as a totality. TIDYING UP STATUTES AND REGULATIONS Chapter 6 of the report recommends measures for tidying up statutes and regulations. With re spect to the statutes, an important step was tå ken in the first report of the Committee, leading to the repealing of 321 outdated statutes by the Storting. This represented approximately 30% of the total number of Norwegian laws. With minor exceptions, one has today through Law data and the compilation of statutes in force a complete inventory of all statutes in force. The Committee encourages the legislator not to pass provisions in the form of a statute where not ne cessary in order to retain the ef ficiency of statu tes as a management strategy, and to secure well organised legislation. An improved structure in statutes and re gulations is one strategy to improve availabi lity. The Committee formulates in Chapter 10 the suggested amendments to the Public Ad ministration Act. A key element in regulatory management is a central data base containing statutes and regulations in authentic text. Ideally this should have both positive and negative cer tainty: A provision contained in the data base is in force in the form represented, and a pro vision not found in the data base is by law not in force. This is, however, not proposed at this time. The Committee has in addition proposals to secure a tidy legislative structure: - The term "provisional statute" should not be used when the statute itself does

however, not proposed at this time. The Committee has in addition proposals to secure a tidy legislative structure: - The term "provisional statute" should not be used when the statute itself does

Bedre struktur i lovverket not contain a sunsetting clause. All exis ting "provisional statutes" should be amended by removing the term "provisi onal" from the title. Statutes which are expected to lose their function after tude that structural or general considerations have too low priority in the later stages when designing new regulations. The Committee the refore emphasizes the need to strengthen these arguments for regulation as a management strategy. Educational initiatives, as well as other actions to improve the understanding of regulatory managers are important. More com prehensive review procedures are proposed: some time, may be termed "provisional" and include a sunsetting clause. - Statutes assenting to the ratification of international agreements should contain a clause specifying that the statute is re pealed automatically when the ratifica tion has been made. The major proposals are: - There should be a duty to mf orm the Le gislative Department of the Ministry of Justice of planned statutory reforms in order to have an assessment of the structural aspects. The mandate of com missions, working parties etc should be reviewed by this Department. - The form of add-on statutes should be avoided. If it is obvious that the additio nal provisions will be in force for some time, and there are exceptional reasons for not integrating these provisions in the statute itself, the provisions should take the form of a provisional statute. - The ministries, working parties and committees must submit drafts for ma jor statutes to the Legislative Depart ment as soon as appropriate. With respect to regulations, the Committee sees a need for drastic action. The Committee therefore proposes: - In all possible cases, an official short tit le should be adopted for the statute. It should be permissible to exclude the date when citing a statute both using the full and the short title. - A new provision should be made part of the Public Administration Act (section 39) specifying that a regulation does not enter into force before integrated in a computerized data base. This implies ne gative security for all regulations issued after this provision enters into force. - In numbering the sections of a statute, one should use the traditional scheme of se quential numbering throughout the statu te. The sections should be divided into pa ragraphs and sentences. Paragraphs may be numbered where appropriate. - A statute is adopted containing a guillo tine rule repealing all regulations not integrated in the Lawdata data base within a certain date. The principle of negative security is thus extended to the regulations already in force. - The Committee advises the editors of le gal information systems like the Official Legal Gazette, Lawdata and the compi lation of statutes in force to include tables of contents in the statutes. - A general review and re-structuring should be undertaken. This should be the responsibility of the ministries, but the Cabinet should appoint an indepen dent Committee to coordinate this work. - There should be a provision in the regu lation on regulatory management that statutes should not enter into force at once unless this is strictly necessary. - Instructions and internal provisions should be reviewed to create a total in ventory of which instructions and con tracts are in force. Instructions and con tracts should be included in the same data base system as the statutes and re gulations. In the same way delegated die cions should be included. - Statutes only dealing with the entry into force of another statute should be avoi ded. If entry into force requires statutory action, an amending statute should be adopted, where the statute to enter into force is amended to include its own date or procedure for entering into force. - Procedures for external review should be developed to improve the structure and improve the quality of drafting in the regulations. PROCEDURES FOR REGULATORY MANAGEMENT In Chapter 7 the Committee puts forward a number of proposals for amended procedures in the different stages of regulatory management. A major conclusion is that the structural argu ments should be part of the work as early as possible. One might in this way correct errors at the very start, but the Committee also main tains that it is a problem of considerable magni- - The Ministry of Local Government should enf orce suf ficient control over the drafting of municipal regulations. The county governor may act as an advisor and control the adoption of regulations in the municipalities of a region. - For certain issues, standards for regula tions should be developed. Vedlegg 29 priate that the relevant ministries are responsible. DEVELOPING THE LEGISLATION The decision to adopt a regulation should be tåken at the highest possible level in a government agency. In Chapter 8 the Committee discusses issues related to the overall development of the le gislation. It considers what substantive provi sions should be adopted as formal statutes, and the appropriate length of a statute. The Committee emphazises that in areas where a comprehensive regulation is necessary, as many of the central provisions of practical im portance should be contained within one sta tute. The Committee maintains that the inclu sion of important provisions in regulations has to be justified by the degree of detail ne cessary, or the need for frequent amendments. The Committee also comments on the Nordic tradition of including normative statements important to the interpretation of the statute in the legislative history. It is important that the legislators are concerned with the effect of this technique. A regulation should not give authority to a subordinate agency to amend the regu lation. If delegation to issue certain pro visions is required, a delegation clause should be included in the regulation. Exemptions from the duty to publish re gulations in the Public Administration Act (section 38(3)) should be repealed. The possibility of publishing other pro visions than statutes and regulations in the Official Legal Gazette should be bet ter utilised. When starting a regulatory reform pro cess, the agency in question should com municate this to those concerned as ear ly as possible, also other agencies res ponsible for related issues. The Committee indicates that provisions should be grouped in larger units than cur rently is the practice. This means that the Committee favours rather lengthy statutes. Fragmented provisions reduce, according to the view held by the Committee, the possibili ty of navigating within the legislation both for the users and for the legislators. The Ministry of Labour and Government Administration and the Ministry of Justi ce should have a general responsibility for regulatory management training and education. The provisions governing regulatory re form should secure an assessment of the structural issues. There should be deve loped a check-list for regulatory review. For the process of consultation or "hea ring" to function according to its objec tive, it should be used with care. Regu latory drafts should be referred to those concerned, and not to others. This should be emphazised in the provisions governing regulatory reform. General opinions on the length of the sta tutes are, however, of little value to those en trusted with the drafting of a statute within a specific area. The most important issue is how the statutes should be integrated. The Com mittee maintains that the provisions should be integrated to ease the use for the normative subjects concerned. The Committee is general ly in agreement with the basic structure of the current legislation, which is organized accor ding to social sectors or social activities. The legislation ought to be structured in such a way that a sectoral statute contains as large a fraction as possible of the provisions applying to that sector. But also a collection of provisi ons applying to activities or a chain of activi ties may be an appropriate organizational scheme. The legislation on the såles of goods or court procedures are examples of the latter. The Official Legal Gazette should be developed to give a crisper image which is more friendly to the reader. The provisions governing regulatory re form should require an assessment of whether major reforms demand special publicity arrangements. One should develop appropriate systems for controlling that regulations achieve their objectives. The Commission sug gests that the system of the Ministry of Justice for ex post control of provisions may be an appropriate basis. There are instances where it would be ap propriate to integrate statutes on the basis of other criteria in order to secure consistency and avoid repetition, for instance with respect to general legal issues. The Statute on Expro priation and the Public Administration Act are examples. But the Committee suggests re straint in grouping provisions according to abstract criteria when the title of the statute is a poor description of the substance. The Committee emphasises that the reduced acces sibility flowing from the division of la w into In addition the Committee discusses substantive aspects of regulations, like the impact in economic terms on the pri vate and the public sectors, unjustified inconsistencies, more than one regula tion for the same issue, etc. A major au dit of the regulations should be conside red at the same time as the proposed ti dying up of the regulations.

inconsistencies, more than one regula tion for the same issue, etc. A major au dit of the regulations should be conside red at the same time as the proposed ti dying up of the regulations.

A SURVEY OF STATUTES IN FORCE In Chapter 9 the Committee has discussed the existing statutes. Based on the criteria discus sed in the general part of the report, the Com mittee has attempted to advise on structural improvements within different areas. The Committee has tried to make its suggestions in a form which may constitute part of future work on regulatory reform, including propo sals for change which may be put into effect in the short term perspective. A common feature of the proposals is the strategy for grouping provisions relating to a sector of society or activity. In other words, it is proposed to depart from the current situation where many provisions are frag mented and therefore difficult to survey. An example is the statutes on taxation. The Committee suggests that all statutes on tax ation should be integrated. As a minimum standard within the area the Committee sug gests that there is no need for more than three statutes: One for the basis of taxation, one for the collection of taxes, and one go verning tax administration. Within many areas the Committee suggests a choice between different strategies. With re spect to the legislation on levies and charges one must choose between integrating the pro visions in the legislation governing the rele vant sector, or group the provisions in one sta tute. The Committee suggests that in order to promote knowledge of the law, the provisions ought to be integrated in the legislation gover ning the action or activities on which a charge is levied. With respect to more general, or fis cal, levies, the Committee suggests an integra tion of the provisions in one statute. A similar strategy is suggested for the criminal law, where one must choose whether the penal pro visions should be integrated in the general cri minal code, or in the relevant statutes. In some instances the Committee suggests major changes in the current structure in or der to improve the knowledge of the law. With respect to the access of the public to land and fields, the Committee suggests that the large number of provisions which are distributed throughout the legislation should be integrated into one statute. Based on the today's principal statute - the Act on Out door Life - the Committee discusses a num ber of provisions which should be integrated into this act. The Committee emphasises that dividing the provisions of one area into several statutes should be avoided. The Committee is quite ne gative to the proposal for new statutes within areas where comprehensive legislation already exists. A common feature of the proposals of the Committee is the integration of minor sta tutes into the major sta tute for an area. The long list of concrete suggestions are, of course, specific for the current Norwegian si tuation. Some examples are mentioned below to illustrate the thrust of the suggestions made by the Committee: - One statute for the territory - One statute for Spitzbergen - Integration of the Public Administra tion Act, the Freedom of Information Act, the Act Governing the Publication of the Official Legal Gazette, the Act on the Parliamentary Ombudsman for Pu blic Administration, and the Act Gover ning Language Usage in Public Admi nistration. - Integration and consolidation of the provisions relating to the church. - Integration of labour law in one act for Employment Contracts, one act on In dustrial Disputes, and one act on Safety at Work. - One act on Health Care, and integration and consolidation of the provisions on confidentiality within health and social care. - The statutes on pensions should be inte grated. - One act on Financial Enterprises, one on State Banks, and one on Lottery. - General provisions on export and im port ought to be integrated in one act. - Requirements for food and food additi ves should be integrated in one act. - The provisions relating to fresh water fisheries should be integrated in one act. - One act on Salt Water Fisheries and the catching of sea mammals, and one act on the Trade in Fish and Taxes levied on this trade. - One act on Animal Diseases. - One act on Forestry, one on the Bree ding of Domestic Animals, one on Plants, Plant diseases and Concentrated Cattle Food. - One act on Domesticated Reindeer. - For provisions relating to property the Committee suggests one act concerning rights to real property, and one act con cerning rights in moveables. - Consolidation of several statutes into the act on Planning and Construction. - A single act on Licences for Trade. - One act on Minerals.
